title: María Pía Santibáñez
text:
I am a fourth-year PhD student in Economics at the Universidad de Chile.
My research interest lies at the intersection of applied microeconomics, labor economics, development economics and Economic History. I am particularly interested in understanding how family environments, public institutions, and social disadvantage influence children’s development and long-term outcomes.
Before beginning my PhD, I studied at Boston University and Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María.
My current research agenda examines children’s life trajectories and the mechanisms through which economic and social disadvantages are transmitted across generations.
You can download my latest Curriculum Vitae here.
Feel free to reach out at marsantiba@fen.uchile.cl.

title: Research
text:
Status: PhD thesis chapter / Working paper
Draft available upon request.
This study examines intergenerational associations in reported offending in Chile, linking administrative records for the 2010 birth cohort to parental justice-system and school records. The sample comprises adolescents with exactly one registered mother and one registered father; the outcome equals one if the adolescent is named as an alleged offender between January 2024 and March 2025, after reaching the minimum age of criminal responsibility. Parental histories are measured through the day before the child’s 14th birthday.
Any parental reported-offense history is positively associated with adolescent justice-system contact. The association rises sharply with the number and legal severity of parental offenses and is larger for boys, histories involving both registered parents, and offenses associated with a recorded custodial sentence. Multiple-type histories produce the largest typology estimate; neither drug-only nor domestic-violence-only (violencia intrafamiliar, VIF) histories account for the largest associations. The results show that early adolescent justice-system contact is concentrated among families with broader, more persistent, and more serious parental records.

title: Research
text:
Work in Progress

Parental Sanctions and Children’s Outcomes: Evidence from Prosecutorial Assignment
Status: Work in progress
This project studies how criminal cases involving a mother or father affect their children’s educational and social outcomes. In Chile, cases are allocated to prosecutors within local offices according to duty schedules, offense specialization, and workload-balancing rules. The empirical design examines whether, within narrowly defined assignment cells, these rules generate conditionally exogenous exposure to prosecutors who differ in the severity of the penalties they request, and whether this variation shifts final case outcomes, including acquittal and the type and severity of sanctions imposed. Outcomes include school dropout, grade repetition, academic performance, adolescent pregnancy, and subsequent justice-system contact among children younger than 18.
